result: KV1.8 is necessary for gK,L in type I hair cells. Knockout of KV1.8 eliminates the characteristic large transient inward current and low-voltage-activated conductance (gK,L) in type I HCs, with >10-fold reduction in maximal conductance and >40 mV positive shift in voltage dependence.
evaluation: All reviewers explicitly affirm this finding. Reviewer 1 states the study 'provides direct evidence showing that KV1.8 channels provide the basis for several potassium currents' and calls it 'an important finding because the nature of the channels underpinning the unusual potassium conductance gK,L in type I hair cells has been under scrutiny for many years.' Reviewer 3 notes 'strong evidence that Kv1.8 subunits are major contributors to the unusual K+ conductance in type I hair cells' and that 'gK,L was completely abolished in Kv1.8-deficient mice.' The experimental evidence is described as 'compelling' with 'rigorous' analysis.

result: KV1.8 is necessary for fast-inactivating (gA) and a substantial portion of delayed rectifier (gDR) currents in type II hair cells. Knockout eliminates gA and reduces gDR by 30-50% across all zones, with gene dosage effects observed in heterozygotes.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly support this finding as a key and surprising result. Reviewer 3 states 'The surprising observation was that in the absence of Kv1.8 potassium channels, the outward potassium current in type II hair cells was also largely reduced' and notes that 'Kv1.8-/- mice lacked an inactivating A conductance and had reduced delayed rectifier conductance compared to controls.' Reviewer 2 notes the authors 'find that this same channel protein appears to function in type II vestibular hair cells as well, contributing to other macroscopic conductances.' The data are described as providing 'strong evidence' with comprehensive characterization.

result: gK,L confers very negative resting potentials (~-87 mV), extremely low input resistances (~50 MΩ), and fast membrane time constants in type I HCs. Loss of KV1.8 results in depolarized resting potential (~-63 mV), ~20-fold increase in input resistance (~1400 MΩ), and slower voltage responses.
evaluation: Reviewers accept these findings without challenge. Reviewer 2 notes that 'Kv1.8 may provide especially low input resistance and short time constants to facilitate encoding of more rapid head movements' and that the study demonstrates how KV1.8-dependent channels 'strongly shape receptor potentials in ways that promote temporal fidelity.' The comprehensive characterization of passive membrane properties and their functional consequences is acknowledged as part of the rigorous experimental approach.

result: Residual outwardly rectifying conductances in KV1.8-null HCs of both types include KV7 channels, demonstrated by ~50% block with XE991. These KV7 conductances have similar voltage dependence and density across HC types and genotypes.
evaluation: Reviewer 4 raises a significant concern about alignment between pharmacological and immunocytochemistry data: 'XE991 (Kv7 channel blocker) decreases remaining K+ conductance in type I and type II hair cells from null mice supporting the presence of Kv7 channels in hair cells (Fig. 7)... However, immunolabelling indicates Kv7.4 channels on the inner face of calyx terminals adjacent to hair cells (Fig. 5). Some reconciliation of these findings is needed.' This discrepancy between functional evidence (XE991 sensitivity) and localization data (immunostaining showing KV7.4 in calyx rather than hair cells) creates uncertainty about the interpretation.

result: The distinct biophysical properties of KV1.8-dependent conductances (non-inactivating gK,L in type I vs. fast-inactivating gA in type II) may reflect heteromultimerization with different KV subunits, particularly KV1.4 in type II cells to confer fast inactivation.
evaluation: Reviewer 4 explicitly identifies this as a major unresolved question: 'if Kv1.8 is a major player and pore-forming subunit in type I and type II cells (and cochlear inner hair cells as shown by Dierich et al. 2020) how are subunits modified to produce channels with very different properties? A role for Kv1.4 channels (gA) is proposed in type II hair cells based on previous findings in bird hair cells. However, hair cell specific partner interactions with Kv1.8 that result in GK,L in type I hair cells and Cs+ impermeable, inactivating currents in type II hair cells remain for the most part unexplored.' This represents a key mechanistic gap acknowledged by the reviewer.

result: KV1.8-dependent conductances increase the speed and damping of voltage responses in both HC types, promoting temporal fidelity. In type II HCs, absence of KV1.8 increases electrical resonance (higher Qe in knockouts: 1.33 vs 0.59-0.66 in controls) without changing resting potential.
evaluation: Reviewers accept these functional characterizations. Reviewer 2 notes that 'Kv1.8 may provide especially low input resistance and short time constants to facilitate encoding of more rapid head movements' and that the channels 'strongly shape receptor potentials in ways that promote temporal fidelity rather than electrical tuning.' Reviewer 4 acknowledges 'the impact of these conductances on membrane responses to current steps is studied in current clamp' as part of the comprehensive analysis. The data are treated as supporting the functional role of KV1.8 in temporal processing.

result: KV1.8 immunoreactivity is present along basolateral membranes of both HC types in control utricles and absent in knockout utricles, confirming specific expression in hair cell membranes.
evaluation: Reviewers accept the immunolocalization data as supporting the electrophysiological findings. Reviewer 4 notes that 'immunostaining data are presented' as part of the evidence bolstering conclusions from biophysical studies. The comparison between control and null tissue is acknowledged as demonstrating selective expression, though the KV7.4 localization issue (discussed in another result) creates some interpretive complexity.

result: During postnatal development (P5-P20), type I HCs transition from conventional delayed rectifier properties to mature gK,L properties, while type II HCs express gA at all ages with increased inactivation after P18. KV1.8 deletion does not affect immature type I HC currents.
evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge the developmental analysis without raising concerns. Reviewer 4 notes that 'Voltage-dependent K+ currents are rigorously characterized at a range of different ages' as part of the comprehensive experimental approach. The finding that immature currents are KV1.8-independent helps clarify the developmental role of this channel subunit.

result: Type I HCs from KV1.8 knockout mice have smaller membrane capacitances (4-5 pF) than heterozygotes (6 pF) or wildtype (6-7 pF), though soma sizes are unchanged, suggesting the difference may not reflect true surface area changes.
evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge this observation. It is presented as a measured parameter that is acknowledged but not extensively discussed by reviewers, suggesting acceptance of the data while recognizing the interpretation remains somewhat uncertain given the lack of corresponding morphological changes.

result: KV1.8 knockout mice show absent or delayed vestibular-evoked potentials but appear healthy and develop normally, with healthy hair cells observed in recordings.
evaluation: Reviewer 4 explicitly requests additional behavioral characterization: 'A previous paper reported that a vestibular evoked potential was abnormal in Kv1.8-/- mice (Lee et al. 2013) as briefly mentioned (lines 94-95). It would be really interesting to know if any vestibular-associated behaviors and/or hearing loss were observed in the mice populations. If responses are compromised at the sensory hair cell level across different zones, degradation of balance function would be anticipated and should be elucidated.' This indicates the reviewer views the functional consequences at the organismal level as incompletely characterized.
